item.title: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn’t seen for decades
item.description:
Congenital measles can be fatal, and survivors require monitoring for years.

Pennsylvania’s health department issueda health alertMonday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn’t been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory.

The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania.

As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though thelatest reported deathis still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally).

The Pennsylvania health department did not immediately respond to a request for information from Ars Technica. Butreporting from The 19thearlier this month put the number of measles cases during pregnancy at 53. At least one case of congenital measles led to a death; the first death reported in the current outbreak was ina newborn baby boy, who died immediately after birth while his mother was severely ill with measles.

Pregnant people who have not been vaccinated against measles nor previously had the infection are susceptible. A case of measles during pregnancy increases the risk of hospitalization, pneumonia, the need for oxygen support or mechanical ventilation, and death. It also increases the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, and preterm labor. The MMR vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because it is a live attenuated vaccine and poses a theoretical risk of causing an infection in a fetus. If a pregnant person is exposed to the virus, they’re recommended to receive intravenous immunoglobulin to help protect against infection—but only if it is given within six days of exposure.

If there’s a measles infection during pregnancy, the measles virus can pass to a fetus in utero or can transmit during or just after birth, leading to a congenital case. These cases can vary widely in symptoms and severity. Some babies will remain asymptomatic while others develop severe, multisystem disease and death. Some common symptoms of congenital measles include fever and jaundice. They can also develop the telltale measles rash, but it is sometimes delayed or atypical given a newborn’s underdeveloped immune system. Other symptoms can include low platelet counts, pneumonia, and neurologic complications.

Even if a newborn survives the acute infection, they are at risk of long-term complications. These include immune amnesia, a type of immunosuppression in which the measles virus destroys immune cells and adaptive responses. They are also at risk of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a progressive, fatal neurological disorder that can strike years after an infection.

The alert warns that babies with congenital measles need long-term clinical follow-up and monitoring for these neurologic and immunologic complications, and parents need counseling on how to spot early signs of SSPE, which include seizures, regression in milestones, and academic difficulties in older children.

item.title: Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos
item.description:
The climax for MMX will come in 2029, when the spacecraft will attempt up to two landings on Phobos.

Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System.

The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan.

The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan’s flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan’s heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date.

The rocket’s upper stage accelerated the MMX spacecraft to a top speed of more than 24,000 mph, fast enough to break free of Earth’s gravitational pull for the 10-month voyage to Mars. The nearly 9,900-pound (4.5-metric ton) spacecraft—two-thirds of its mass comprised of propellant—separated from the H3 rocket about 71 minutes after liftoff.

Hiroshi Yamakawa, president of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), declared the launch a success. “A long journey of five years has just started,” Yamakawa said.

MMX established contact with ground controllers, unfurled its solar panels, and was in a “very stable condition” soon after separating from the H3 rocket, according to Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, the mission’s project manager at JAXA. “So far, so good.”

“The MMX [mission] we launched today is a challenging mission aiming for the world’s first sample return from the Martian moons,” said Yoshihiro Seki, Japan’s science minister. “We hope that the results obtained through this mission will contribute to the development of our nation’s space science and exploration technology.”

The mission to the Martian moons builds on Japan’s success in leading the Hayabusa andHayabusa 2 missions, the world’s first two spacecraft to bring back pristine specimens from asteroids. Scientists believe Phobos could itself be an asteroid that was captured into orbit around Mars billions of years ago. One of MMX’s science goals is finding out if that theory is correct.

With the Hayabusa missions, sample returns from deep space have become a “speciality” for Japan’s space program, Kawakatsu said. For MMX, Japan attracted contributions from NASA and space agencies in Europe.

“We have a proven track record of success in these areas,” Kawakatsu said. “Because of this, I believe they are participating with the understanding that if they want to conduct celestial body sample returns, joining a mission led by Japan is more certain to succeed than the US or Europe launching their own missions.”

MMX will spend about three years in the vicinity of Mars after arriving there next August, conducting a series of encounters with the Martian moons Phobos and Deimos.Phobos is the larger of the two, with a lumpy, potato-like shape, an average diameter of 14 miles (22 kilometers), and a surface area comparable to the city of Houston.

Upon reaching Mars, MMX will jettison its propulsion module, dead weight after burning all its fuel to enter orbit around the red planet. That will leave the main section of the MMX spacecraft and its four-legged landing gear, known as the exploration module, to move closer to Phobos.

The moon’s gravity is too weak and the pull of Martian gravity too strong for the MMX spacecraft to enter into a stable orbit around Phobos. Instead, the spacecraft will fly in a so-called quasi-satellite orbit, remaining bound to Mars while still able to maneuver around Phobos.

The mission’s reconnaissance of Phobos will culminate in late 2028 or early 2029, when the MMX mothership will release a small rover to drop onto Phobos. The four-wheeled robot,named Idefix, is a contribution from the French and German space agencies. Idefix, the size of a large shoebox, will attempt to drive around Phobos for up to 100 days while grappling with the moon’s rough topography and tenuous gravity, less than one-thousandth that of Earth’s.

The climax for MMX will come later in 2029, when the main spacecraft will attempt up to two landings on Phobos. The probe’s landing gear is designed to absorb energy of each landing to mitigate the risk of tipping over or bouncing back into space, a real concern with the feeble and uneven gravity field on Phobos.

The spacecraft will stay on the surface of Phobos for several hours, using two independent mechanisms to capture samples from the Martian moon. A coring drill on the end of the probe’s robotic arm will scoop out a cigar-shaped specimen, while a NASA-provided pneumatic sampler on one of the craft’s landing legs will fire a cartridge of high-pressure nitrogen gas to sweep bits of Phobos in a collection canister.

All told, scientists expect MMX to retrieve at least 10 grams, or one-third of an ounce, of material from Phobos. After climbing back into space, MMX will discard its landing gear and fire its engines in 2030 to head for Earth, where it will guide a sample return capsule toward a remote landing zone in South Australia in 2031.

Scientists will recover the samples for analysis in laboratories in Japan. US researchers will get 15 percent of the Phobos specimens in return for NASA’s contributions to the MMX mission, which include one of the spacecraft’s samplers and a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer to measure the elemental makeup of the Martian moons.

“One of the most intriguing questions about Phobos and Deimos is simply why these two little moons are there in the first place,” said Tom Statler, lead scientist for solar system small bodies at NASA. “In some ways, they resemble asteroids from the outer part of the asteroid belt, so they could be asteroids that were captured by Mars’s gravity. But there are other lines of evidence pointing to these moons being remnants of a giant impact early in Mars’s history.”

“By going to the Martian moons, studying them up close, and bringing samples back to Earth, we’ll be able to determine whether Phobos material is more consistent with an asteroid composition or with debris created by a collision involving Mars,” Statler said.

Phobos is roughly 40 times closer to Mars than our Moon is to Earth. Its proximity to Mars means there is a chance MMX might scoop up traces of the red planet itself that rained down on Phobos after its formation or capture. This could offer a taste of what’s to come when scientists finally get their hands on specimens directly from the surface of Mars,a significantly more difficult undertakingthan a sample return from Phobos.

The reconnaissance of Phobos by MMX could also help future mission planners consider whether the moon is a suitable location for human exploration, perhaps as a stopover between Earth and Mars,Kawakatsusaid.

MMX is not the first mission to attempt a sample return from Phobos. Russia’s Phobos-Grunt sample return mission failed soon after launch in 2011, before it could set off for Mars. The Soviet Union launched two spacecraft to Mars equipped with Phobos landers in 1988, but ground teams lost contact with both spacecraft before they completed their missions.

With MMX, scientists hope to finally acquire the ground truth on the Martian moons they have sought for decades.

“Basically, these objects look more like primitive asteroids than anything else, but the data is coming from remote sensing from far away,” said Patrick Michel, a French asteroid scientist and co-leader of the Idefix rover project. “That cannot really tell us exactly what are the properties, as we can do with a sample return in the lab.”

“The goal of the mission is effectively to reveal the origin of the Martian moons,” Michel said. “If we understand the origin, that will tell us something about the early phases of the Solar System.”

item.title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
item.description:
Slate’s first showroom sells the promise. Mass production will determine the rest.

As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips.

Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even pre-order a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit.

Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is abare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950. It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars got to go for aride in a Slate Truck over the summer, but we haven’t had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate.

Upon walking into the showroom on a Monday morning, the first thing I noticed was a marquee-style sign on the wall boldly and brightly serving as a price tag for the black truck parked in the middle of the showroom. The vibe was industrial-barn-chic-meets-SoHo-loft. Three other people were there, and another shopper entered as I left. One man alternated between sitting in the cab, peering at the truck as he walked around it, and peppering Manager of Customer Experience Steve Purdy with questions.

The showroom has been open since October 15, launching with a three-day event that offered ridealongs. Interest has been strong, Purdy told me, and while he couldn’t provide sales numbers, he said the response has been “incredible.”

“We’re really happy with the number of [$300] deposits we’ve gotten since we opened,” Purdy said.

I was hoping there would be at least two Slate Trucks on site, so I could compare build quality between trucks and check things like panel gaps, window operation, and chassis creaks. But only one truck was on display. And it wasn’t close to a production model; rather, the black Slate Truck was a hand-built, older prototype with a black wrap (the Slate Truck base color is gray). The bed and passenger sides were cordoned off, but the driver-side door was open so shoppers could hop in and check out the interior.

It was bigger than I expected—to my eye, roughly the size of a Hyundai Santa Cruz. The tailgate was down, and it felt reassuringly sturdy when I pressed down on it. The 5-foot-long (152.4 cm) bed floor looked and felt durable, not much different from any other pickup on the market.

The exterior passed the eye test, with the panels appearing well-fitted. The doors sat flush with the surrounding body panels when closed. Of course, I was looking at a prototype carefully built to be poked and prodded by automotive reporters and the general public, so the level of fit and finish was no surprise. The challenge for Slate will be getting consistent build quality with minimal panel gaps, watertight seals, consistent door-to-fender transitions, and hood/frunk alignment. The Slate assembly line in Warsaw, Indiana, is still making prototyping runs at this point, Purdy told me, and the company is hoping to start on production models “soon.”

I hopped inside the cab once I got the opportunity, and the door closed with a solid-sounding “thunk.” It’s spartan inside, with a small screen for the instrument panel, a phone holder, physical climate controls, and window winders. The seats were both supportive and comfortable, and, after moving the seat, I had ample legroom. While the seat slid back and forth smoothly, the seatback recline lever on the side didn’t work.

Beyond the default Blank Slate body style, Slate offers two SUV options—the Squareback SUV and Fastback SUV—and an open-air kit. I asked Purdy if they were selling any of the SUVs. “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,” he said. “And then they’re customizing their trucks in the Slate Garage.”

Being able to order online and have the truck delivered is a major attraction for those who can’t stand “the kabuki dance of f***ery at a dealership,” as one of my colleagues put it. But if you want to do all that at the Slate Experience Center, staffers will sit down and help you configure your customized Slate. There is a wall with removable dashboard panels across the color spectrum and a couple of miniature models of the cab with tiny, colored panels to help customers decide on the details.

Purdy told me that Slate is staying the course with the $24,950 sticker price. But will customers actually get their Slate Trucks this year as the company promised? “We will be ship some trucks by the end of the year,” Purdy said. “Those will go to investors and employees, with early-orderers receiving their Slate Trucks in early 2027.

For service, Slate will be usingRepairPal. Owners will be able to choose from 4,000 shops, some of which can service the high-voltage electrical systems and others limited to body damage, Purdy said. For scratches or minor dings from fender benders, owners can replace the exterior body panels themselves. Pricing for replacement parts has yet to be finalized. And Slate is confident the plastic body panels will weather climate extremes without a hitch. “We’re a Michigan company,” Purdy reminded me.

Monday morning is not exactly prime time for dealership traffic, but a handful of prospective customers were in the showroom, which is a promising sign. While there is no shortage of electrified pickup trucks on the market, there is a shortage of affordable ones. At $25,000, the Slate Truck costs far less than a Rivian R1T, Tesla Cybertruck, Chevy Silverado EV, or any currently shipping battery-electric truck. It could be a breakout hit—especially if Slate can beatFord’s sub-$30,000 Fathom pickupto market.

But the sleek-looking showroom and an attractive prototype still face a production reality check. Tesla hadsignificant quality control problems with early Model Ys, with customers receiving cars with loose seats and broken seatbelts, and some Cybertrucks have shipped withmisaligned panel gaps. A new player is entering the game, but production is still on the (near) horizon, and no one knows if the Slate Trucks delivered to customers will live up to the promise of the carefully hand-built prototypes. People are definitely very interested in Slate. Now it’s time to deliver.
